Nurse training should encompass safe use of AI tools, recognition of algorithmic limitations, ethical decision-making in AI-mediated care and skills for interpreting AI-generated recommendations within clinical context.
Second, nursing workforce development should integrate AI literacy, algorithmic-bias awareness and digital ethics as core competencies in both pre-service and continuing education.

Co-design processes should be linguistically accessible and should prioritise the involvement of women who have used or are likely to use MCH services, including those from marginalised communities at greatest risk of digital exclusion.
Use participatory, culturally responsive and language-appropriate co-design; nurses should facilitate sustained community dialogue and feedback loops rather than token consultation.

Embed longitudinal, equity-stratified monitoring of clinical, implementation and patient-reported outcomes; run feedback loops to revalidation and re-design; schedule periodic recalibration and bias re-audit; apply explicit stop or roll-back criteria.
Conduct longitudinal evaluation of clinical outcomes, implementation outcomes (adoption, fidelity, sustainability), costs, safety, equity effects and patient experience.

National digital health strategies in LMICs should require mandatory local validation of AI models before MCH deployment, establish nurse-inclusive AI governance bodies, and integrate AI ethics and digital competency training into nursing curricula.
Nurses should contribute systematically to AI system design, workflow integration, community engagement, policy development and outcome evaluation.

unlisted_practices: Provide inclusive, low-cost, community-based digital access pathways such as shared-device and community health worker intermediary models and offline-capable platforms so AI does not exclude women lacking devices or connectivity.

Invest in foundational infrastructure (electricity, connectivity, interoperable information systems) and sequence AI adoption within broader health system strengthening rather than diverting resources.
Establish transparent data governance covering informed consent respecting community norms, data minimisation, secure storage, and harm reporting for sensitive maternal and child health data.
Position nurses as co-designers and gatekeepers of AI, treating AI outputs as advisory inputs that support rather than replace nursing judgement and relational care.
International donors should fund equity-sensitive evaluations of AI-assisted programmes rather than proliferation of unvalidated tools.

screen.reason: This is a perspective/framework paper proposing an equity-centred, nurse-led conceptual framework and implementation pathway for AI in community maternal and child health nursing.
